==Funerary Goods== The most commonly recovered grave goods include iron weapons such as swords, bows, and arrows, and earthenware items such as {{ill|Haji pottery|en|Haji pottery|WD=Q5639938|lt=Haji pottery}} and {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}, with iron arrowheads—particularly those of the {{ill|Keitō type|ja|圭頭鏃|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keitō type|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}—appearing very frequently. Additionally, items such as {{ill|snake-like swords|ja|蛇行剣|1=Dakōken|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/snake-like swords|13=User:Immanuelle/Dakōken|qq=}} and various irregularly shaped iron implements are characteristic. There are also cases where especially luxurious grave goods, including jade objects, armor ({{ill|Japanese armour|en|Japanese armour|WD=Q3671179|lt=kacchū}}), equestrian gear ({{ill|Horse tack|en|Horse tack|WD=Q950799|lt=horse gear}}), and mirrors, are interred; tombs containing such goods are considered comparable to elite head tombs found in keyhole-shaped Kofuns.
==Distribution== The distribution of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs extends from the northern limit at the Ushimoku Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in Ōaza Kamie, {{ill|Takanabe, Miyazaki|en|Takanabe, Miyazaki|WD=Q1206737|lt=Takanabe Town}}, {{ill|Koyu District, Miyazaki|en|Koyu District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132169|lt=Koyugu District}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, to the southern limit at the Nakao Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. They are mainly distributed in the Miyazaki Plain, extending into the basins of areas such as {{ill|Miyakonojō|en|Miyakonojō|WD=Q638301|lt=Tosu City}}, {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, and {{ill|Ebino, Miyazaki|en|Ebino, Miyazaki|WD=Q374701|lt=Ebino City}} at the northern foothills of the {{ill|Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja|霧島火山群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 霧島山|1=Mount Kirishima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1319361}}, with the western boundary marked by the Harumura Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in {{ill|Isa, Kagoshima|en|Isa, Kagoshima|WD=Q15736|lt=Isa City}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. Additionally, two tombs have been detected at the Tendōgao site in {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|WD=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, indicating that the northwestern extent of this tomb style reaches into the basin of the {{ill|Kuma River (Japan)|en|Kuma River (Japan)|WD=Q1358183|lt=Kumagawa River}}.
In total, more than 1,000 Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs have been discovered in Miyazaki and Kagoshima Prefectures,<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012"/> with over 300 confirmed in the Ebino City region of western Miyazaki Prefecture.
==Origins and Spread== The initial form of the tomb is thought to be the “Yokuguchi-style Earthen Tomb” that appeared in the latter half of the early Kofun period to the early mid-Kofun period, discovered within a subgroup of the {{ill|Kogihara Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja|小木原地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogihara Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. Thereafter, based on the shape of the burial chamber, these tombs were broadly classified into two categories – the “houseform type” and the “earthen mound type” – which spread across various regions via transmission from the 5th to the 6th centuries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=143"/>
In the Miyazaki Plain and along the coast of the Ōsumi Peninsula at Shibushi Bay, the distribution of keyhole-shaped tumuli overlaps with that of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs; in the inland areas near the Okuchi Basin, their distribution overlaps with that of another southern Kyushu burial style, the {{ill|stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓|1=stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|qq=}} (Underground stone slab tomb).
==Research History== Records of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs date back to the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} and even earlier to the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治期|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}}. In the work ''{{ill|Keirin Manroku|ja|桂林漫録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keirin Manroku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'' by {{ill|Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja|森島（桂川）中良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the younger brother of {{ill|Katsuragawa Hoshū|en|Katsuragawa Hoshū|WD=Q946932|lt=Katsuragawa Hoshu}}, an account from 1789 (the 1st year of {{ill|Kansei|en|Kansei|WD=Q1195131|lt=Kansei}}) describes a farmer in {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}} near the pig mound at {{ill|Inoh-tsuka|ja|猪の塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inoh-tsuka|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|en|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132180|lt=Higashimorokata District}}, {{ill|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|en|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350786|lt=Kunimoto Town}}, Honjō) who, while digging a trench, encountered a horizontal cave with its walls painted vermilion, from which numerous relics were unearthed. Local historian {{ill|Senokuchi Denkurō|ja|瀬之口伝九郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senokuchi Denkurō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} regarded this as the earliest literary reference to an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/> In modern times, research in the field of {{ill|Archaeology|en|Archaeology|WD=Q23498|lt=archaeology}} began, and Senokuchi Denkurō coined the term “Underground-type Tomb” to classify it as one form of Kofun period burial system.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/>
Subsequently, studies have gradually advanced using archaeological methods such as the classification of plan and cross-sectional morphologies, chronological analyses based on grave goods, and examinations of the relationship between these tombs and keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|日高|1958"/><ref name="Sfn|石川|1973"/>
===The “Hayato Burial System” Theory=== Alongside these developments, a theory emerged proposing that Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs, due to their unique structure, concentrated distribution in southern Kyushu, and the fact that southern Kyushu lay on the periphery of the keyhole-shaped tumuli (Kofun culture zone), were the tombs of the “Hayato,” a group historically considered peripheral by the ancient {{ill|Ritsuryō state|ja|律令国家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō state|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 律令制|1=ritsuryō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q742460}}. <ref name="Sfn|高橋|1924"/> In the 1960s–80s, as comprehensive views of the Kofun period emerged, this theory accelerated, with several scholars identifying Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs as representing the burial system of the “Hyūga–Ōsumi Hayato,” the Underground stone slab tomb as that of the “Satsuma Hayato,” and certain tumuli-associated tombs in the southern Satsuma Peninsula as that of the “Ata Hayato.”<ref name="Sfn|小田|1966|p=163"/><ref name="Sfn|乙益|1970"/><ref name="Sfn|上村|1984"/> Their formation was attributed to the region’s volcanic soils, limited flatlands unsuitable for rice cultivation, and its isolation from external influences, leading to cultural stagnation from the Yayoi period onward and the establishment of an independent local sphere. This framework, which depicted the “specialized underground tomb system in southern Kyushu” as “Hayato tombs” in contrast to the expanding dominion of the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato court|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kinship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}}, gradually gained widespread acceptance.
However, by the 1990s, increasing criticism emerged—especially from scholars in Kyushu—questioning the appropriateness of linking Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs with the “Hayato.”
The term “Hayato” first appears in the mythological portions of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}}, and while it is mentioned from the time of Emperor Nintoku, its use as a confirmed historical term is generally recognized only from the 11th month of the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmu period|ja|天武朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu period|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (682 AD, in records of Hayato tributary missions).<ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/> In contrast, the peak of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs was in the 5th to 6th centuries, and they appear to have largely ceased by the mid-7th century. Furthermore, the areas inhabited by groups identified as “Hayato” during the Ritsuryō period were confined to {{ill|Ōsumi Province|en|Ōsumi Province|WD=Q981002|lt=Ōsumi Province}} and {{ill|Satsuma Province|ja|Satsuma Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satsuma Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, excluding {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}}. Thus, if the common burial system reflects a unified cultural group, the inhabitants of Osumi might be considered “Hayato,” whereas those of Hyūga would not. It is argued that the very notion of “Hayato” was a pseudo-ethnic construct, politically created by the Ritsuryō government based on Sinocentric ideology rather than arising from indigenous ethnic differences.<ref name="Sfn|永山|2009|pp=40"/><ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/><ref name="Sfn|東|2001|p=498"/>
Archaeologically, numerous instances have been documented where keyhole-shaped tumuli and Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs coexist, or where Underground Tombs serve as the main burial facility within tumuli, indicating that their relationship cannot be simply explained as a dichotomy between “Yamato” and local forces. Consequently, the equation of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs with “Hayato tombs” has gradually lost support in both archaeological and literary studies.<ref name="Sfn|下山|1995"/><ref name="Sfn|永山|1998|pp=10–11"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2008"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2011"/>
===Research After the “Hayato Burial System” Theory=== From the 2000s onward, research on Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs has increasingly employed extensive excavation data and artifacts to examine these tombs using rigorous archaeological methods, viewing them as a regional burial system of the Kofun period. Detailed discussions now focus on classifications based on structural morphology, chronological models derived from grave goods and distribution patterns, and analyses of the social structure of the regions where these tombs were constructed in relation to keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|第4回九州前方後円墳研究会|2001"/><ref name="Sfn|第6回九州前方後円墳研究会|2003"/>

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:地下式横穴墓]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:地下式横穴墓]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:地下式横穴墓]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11424056]] Wikidata name: underground tunnel tomb [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:16, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:地下式横穴墓の模式図.png|350px|thumb|{{ill|Schematic diagram of an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb|ja|地下式横穴墓の模式図|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Schematic diagram of an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}]] '''Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb''' (地下式横穴墓) is a tomb in which a vertical pit is excavated into the ground, and from that pit a horizontal chamber is dug to construct a burial facility in which the deceased are interred. It is known as a regionally distinctive burial style that appeared during the 5th to 6th centuries of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period}} in southern parts of the {{ill|Kyushu region|ja|九州地方|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyushu region|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九州|1=Kyushu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13987}}, particularly from the southern part of {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}} to the eastern part of {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}.
==Overview== The Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb is situated in the flatlands of the upper portion of a plateau, in contrast to the more widespread {{ill|cave tomb|lt=horizontal cave tombs|ja|横穴墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/cave tomb|qq=}} of the mid to late Kofun period, which were built by excavating into hillsides or cliff faces. In the Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb, a vertical pit is dug to a depth of approximately 2–3 meters, and then excavation proceeds horizontally from the bottom of the pit, ensuring that the burial chamber is constructed at a level below the surface. Thus, by contrast with standard horizontal cave tombs, the term “underground type” is applied.
===Structure=== ; Vertical Pit : The vertical pit (also written as “竪穴”) generally has a plan form that is roughly elliptical or quadrangular with rounded corners and serves as the entrance descending underground. It is speculated that a ladder or similar apparatus was used for ascent and descent; for example, in one Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb at Tomb No. 18 of the {{ill|Okazaki Kofun Group|ja|岡崎古墳群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okazaki Kofun Group|1=Okazaki Kofun Group|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q42581362}} in {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City}}, {{ill|foot-holds|ja|足掛け|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/foot-holds|1=foot-holds|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11636886}} were detected on the wall of the pit. Since burial rites in these tombs often involved secondary interments, the vertical pit was typically not refilled, remaining open or sealed at its top with flagstones or wooden boards. ; Access Passage : The portion leading from the bottom of the vertical pit to the burial chamber is called the “access passage” (羨道); however, when its length is too short to be considered a “passage,” it is sometimes referred to as the “access gate” (羨門). The entrance to the access passage was sealed by stacking flagstones, river stones, or lumps of clay. ; Burial Chamber : The burial chamber (玄室) is excavated as a broad horizontal space deeper within the access passage. Its plan may vary – it can be a long rectangular chamber (wife-entry type), a nearly square chamber, a chamber with a width disproportionately greater than its depth (plain-entry type), or even an elliptical chamber. Some chambers have a domed ceiling, while others feature a triangular ceiling that clearly mimics the roof of a house, decorated with motifs resembling pillars, beams, or horizontal lintels. The remains were interred in an extended posture from the rear of the chamber, and with each subsequent secondary burial the newly interred were placed nearer the entrance. In some cases, during secondary burial, previously interred remains that had become ossified were relocated to the rear wall corner to make room. In certain tombs, the remains were placed directly on the floor; in others, a mortuary platform of rounded stones or a Sarcophagus constructed with flagstones was provided. Alongside the remains, grave goods such as iron weapons, {{ill|Haji pottery|en|Haji pottery|WD=Q5639938|lt=Haji pottery}} and {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}, as well as ornaments, were deposited. Owing to the sealed nature of the underground chamber, these grave goods have generally been preserved in relatively good condition at the time of excavation, largely free from soil degradation and later looting. ; Surface Structures : Generally, there are no surface structures or markers resembling the tumuli of keyhole-shaped Kofuns present on the ground surface. Consequently, the locations of these tombs often went unrecognized by later generations; there are instances where collapse of the burial chamber ceiling led to sudden ground subsidence and subsequent discovery, or where plowing or agricultural improvements caused farm animals or tractors to become caught in a collapsed chamber, leading to accidental discoveries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=139"/> In recent times, surveys of buried cultural assets have sometimes employed ground-penetrating radar to determine the location. Additionally, the {{ill|Board of Education of Miyazaki City|ja|宮崎県都城市|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Board of Education of Miyazaki City|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} has issued warnings on its website regarding sudden ground subsidence in agricultural areas, noting that such events may indicate the presence of an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb.
===Group Structure=== An individual Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb is rarely constructed alone; they are usually found in clusters of 2–3 or even in groups of over 100. Consequently, the archaeological site is typically designated as “[Place Name] + Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group.” Moreover, as mentioned above, there are examples where several Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs form a circular group, or where vertical pits are excavated at the base of tumuli such as keyhole-shaped mounds (【前方後円墳】), with the burial chamber oriented toward the summit of the mound, appearing as if subordinate to or sharing the mound.
==Funerary Goods== The most commonly recovered funerary goods include iron weapons such as swords and bows and arrows, as well as earthenware items such as {{ill|Haji pottery|en|Haji pottery|WD=Q5639938|lt=Haji pottery}} and {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}; notably, iron arrowheads are frequently found, with the majority being of the {{ill|Keitō arrowhead|ja|圭頭鏃|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keitō arrowhead|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} type. Additionally, there are cases where exceptionally luxurious grave goods – including jewelry, armor ({{ill|Japanese armour|en|Japanese armour|WD=Q3671179|lt=kacchū}}), equestrian gear ({{ill|Horse tack|en|Horse tack|WD=Q950799|lt=magugu}}), and mirrors – have been interred. Tombs containing such lavish goods are considered comparable to elite head tombs found in keyhole-shaped Kofuns.
==Distribution== The distribution of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs extends from the northern limit at the Ushimoku Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in the Ōaza Kamie of {{ill|Takanabe, Miyazaki|en|Takanabe, Miyazaki|WD=Q1206737|lt=Takanabe Town}}, {{ill|Koyu District, Miyazaki|en|Koyu District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132169|lt=Koyugu District}} in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, to the southern limit at the Nakao Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho, Agata}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City}} in {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. They are distributed in the basins of the Miyazaki Plain and extend into areas such as {{ill|Miyakonojō|en|Miyakonojō|WD=Q638301|lt=Tosu City}}, {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, and {{ill|Ebino, Miyazaki|en|Ebino, Miyazaki|WD=Q374701|lt=Ebino City}}, at the northern foothills of the {{ill|Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja|霧島火山群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 霧島山|1=Mount Kirishima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1319361}}, with the western limit marked by the Harumura Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in {{ill|Isa, Kagoshima|en|Isa, Kagoshima|WD=Q15736|lt=Isa City}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}} on the western slope of Kirishima. On the Ōsumi Peninsula, they are found along the coast of {{ill|Shibushi Bay|ja|志布志湾|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shibushi Bay|1=Shibushi Bay|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11490886}} from {{ill|Kushima, Miyazaki|en|Kushima, Miyazaki|WD=Q845800|lt=Kushima City}} in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}} to {{ill|Ōsaki, Kagoshima|en|Ōsaki, Kagoshima|WD=Q931439|lt=Osaki Town}} in {{ill|Soo District, Kagoshima|en|Soo District, Kagoshima|WD=Q1043870|lt=Soo District}}, as well as within the inland area of Kanoya City. Slightly removed from the main distribution areas, two tombs have been detected at the Tendōgao site in {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|WD=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, indicating that the northwestern limit of this tomb style extends into the basin of the {{ill|Kuma River (Japan)|en|Kuma River (Japan)|WD=Q1358183|lt=Kumagawa River}}.
The total number of tombs discovered in both Miyazaki and Kagoshima Prefectures exceeds 1,000,<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012"/> with over 300 confirmed in the Ebino City region of western Miyazaki Prefecture.
==Origins and Spread== In the early form of the tomb, the “Yokuguchi-style earthen tomb” that emerged in the latter half of the early Kofun period in a subgroup within the {{ill|Kogihara Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja|小木原地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogihara Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, is considered to be the precursor. Subsequently, based on the shape of the burial chamber, these tombs became broadly categorized into two types – the “houseform type” and the “earthen mound type” – which were transmitted across various prefectures from the 5th to the 6th centuries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=143"/>
In the Miyazaki Plain and along the coast of Shibushi Bay on the Ōsumi Peninsula, the distribution area of keyhole-shaped tumuli overlaps with that of the Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs, and in the inland areas near the Okuchi Basin, the distribution of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs overlaps with that of another southern Kyushu burial style, the {{ill|stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓|1=stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|qq=}} (Underground stone slab tomb).
==Research History== The discovery records of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs date back from the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} to the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治期|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}}, with an account in the work ''{{ill|Keirin Manroku|ja|桂林漫録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keirin Manroku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'' by {{ill|Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja|森島（桂川）中良|lt=Mori Island Nakayoshi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the younger brother of {{ill|Katsuragawa Hoshū|en|Katsuragawa Hoshū|WD=Q946932|lt=Katsuragawa Hoshu}}, noting that in 1789 (the 1st year of {{ill|Kansei|en|Kansei|WD=Q1195131|lt=Kansei}}) a farmer in {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}} near {{ill|Ino-tsuka|ja|猪の塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ino-tsuka|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} ({{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|en|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132180|lt=Higashimorokata District}}, {{ill|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|en|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350786|lt=Kunimoto Town}}, Honjō) discovered a horizontal cave with its walls painted vermilion, from which numerous relics were unearthed. Local historian {{ill|Senokuchi Denkurō|ja|瀬之口伝九郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senokuchi Denkurō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} regarded this as the first literary reference to an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/> In modern times, research in the field of {{ill|Archaeology|en|Archaeology|WD=Q23498|lt=archaeology}} began, and it was Senokuchi Denkurō who coined the term “Underground-type Tomb” and framed it as one form of Kofun period burial style.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/>
Subsequently, archaeological studies employing methods such as plan and cross-sectional classification of the remains, chronological investigations based on grave goods, and analyses of the relationship between these tombs and keyhole-shaped tumuli have gradually advanced.<ref name="Sfn|日高|1958"/><ref name="Sfn|石川|1973"/>
===The “Hayato Burial System” Theory=== Parallel to these developments, a theory emerged suggesting that Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs, owing to their peculiar structure, their concentrated distribution in southern Kyushu, and the fact that southern Kyushu lay on the periphery of the keyhole-shaped tumuli distribution (the Kofun cultural sphere), were the tombs of the “Hayato” – a group regarded in ancient literature as peripheral or “other” tribes by the centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō state|ja|律令国家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō state|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 律令制|1=ritsuryō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q742460}}. <ref name="Sfn|高橋|1924"/> In the 1960s–80s, as comprehensive studies of Kofun period society emerged, this theory accelerated, and several researchers posited that Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs represented the burial system of the “Hyūga–Ōsumi Hayato”, that the {{ill|stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓|1=stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|qq=}} (Underground stone slab tomb) represented the burial system of the “Satsuma Hayato”, and that the “Tateishi Doikombō” found in the southern part of the Satsuma Peninsula represented the burial system of the “Ata Hayato”.<ref name="Sfn|小田|1966|p=163"/><ref name="Sfn|乙益|1970"/><ref name="Sfn|上村|1984"/> Their formation was explained by the fact that the area was characterized by volcanic soils, limited plains unsuitable for rice cultivation, and an environment isolated from the outside world, which resulted in the stagnation of cultural change from the Yayoi period onward and the emergence of an independent local power sphere. This view, portraying a dichotomy between the expanding dominion of the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato court|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kinship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}} (centered in the Kofun cultural sphere) and the “Hayato” – a group created politically and arbitrarily by the Ritsuryō government based on {{ill|Sinocentric ideology|ja|華夷思想|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sinocentric ideology|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 中華思想|1=sinocentrism|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1370788}} – became widely accepted among the general public.
However, from the 1990s onward, many researchers – especially local scholars and academic circles in Kyushu – began to question whether linking Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs with the “Hayato” was appropriate.
In literary sources, the first appearance of the term “Hayato” is found in the mythological sections of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}}, and it appears from the reign of Emperor Nintoku onward; yet as a confirmed historical fact, the use of the term “Hayato” is generally accepted only from the 11th month of the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmu period|ja|天武朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu period|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (682 AD, in records of Hayato tributes) onward.<ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/> In contrast, the heyday of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs was centered on the 5th to 6th centuries, and they persisted only until roughly the mid-7th century. Moreover, the territories inhabited by the groups referred to as “Hayato” during the Ritsuryō period were limited to {{ill|Ōsumi Province|en|Ōsumi Province|WD=Q981002|lt=Ōsumi Province}} and {{ill|Satsuma Province|ja|Satsuma Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satsuma Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, excluding {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}}; if the distribution of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs indeed indicates the habitation of a culturally unified group, then while the inhabitants of Osumi may be considered “Hayato,” those of Hyūga would not. It is argued that the very notion of “Hayato” was a pseudo-ethnic construct created by the Ritsuryō government based on Sinocentric ideology, rather than a concept arising from indigenous power or ethnic differences.<ref name="Sfn|永山|2009|pp=40"/><ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/><ref name="Sfn|東|2001|p=498"/>
From an archaeological standpoint, numerous examples have emerged in which keyhole-shaped tumuli and Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs coexisted, or where Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs served as the primary burial facility within keyhole-shaped tumuli, indicating that the relationship between these two burial styles cannot be adequately explained by a simple dichotomy of “Yamato” versus “local forces.” In this context, the simplistic equation of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs with “Hayato tombs” has increasingly come under criticism.
===Research After the “Hayato Burial System” Theory=== From the 2000s onward, research on Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs has increasingly employed the vast amount of data and artifacts recovered from excavations to examine these tombs in a more archaeological manner as a regional burial system of the Kofun period. Detailed discussions have emerged regarding classification based on structural typology, chronological models derived from grave good assemblages and distribution patterns, and analyses of the social structure of regions where Underground Tombs were constructed in relation to keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|第4回九州前方後円墳研究会|2001"/><ref name="Sfn|第6回九州前方後円墳研究会|2003"/>
Currently, it is becoming increasingly clear that the emergence, development, and spread of this tomb style resulted from the adoption of “horizontal cave–type” burial techniques (both in funerary ideology and technology) brought from the continent. In this region, these techniques were implemented in an underground structure, indicating that this tomb style was not born in isolation in an inhospitable environment but was established through active regional exchange with the {{ill|Korean Peninsula|ja|朝鮮半島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Korean Peninsula|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Korean Peninsula|WD=Q483134}} and the {{ill|Yamato government|ja|ヤマト政権|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato government|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kinship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}}.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012"/>

==Origins of Grave Goods== The most frequently encountered grave goods include iron weapons such as swords and bows and arrows, as well as earthenware such as {{ill|Haji pottery|en|Haji pottery|WD=Q5639938|lt=Haji pottery}} and {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}, with iron arrowheads, particularly those of the {{ill|Keitō type|ja|圭頭鏃|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keitō type|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, appearing in overwhelming numbers. Other notable items include {{ill|snake-like swords|ja|蛇行剣|1=Dakōken|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/snake-like swords|13=User:Immanuelle/Dakōken|qq=}}, various irregularly shaped iron implements, as well as precious items such as jade, armaments ({{ill|Japanese armour|en|Japanese armour|WD=Q3671179|lt=armor}}), equestrian equipment ({{ill|Horse tack|en|Horse tack|WD=Q950799|lt=horse gear}}), and mirrors. Tombs with such lavish grave goods are considered comparable to the elite head tombs found in keyhole-shaped Kofuns.
==Distribution== The distribution of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs extends from the northern limit marked by the Ushimoku Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group at Ōaza Kamie in {{ill|Takanabe, Miyazaki|en|Takanabe, Miyazaki|WD=Q1206737|lt=Takanabe Town}}, {{ill|Koyu District, Miyazaki|en|Koyu District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132169|lt=Koyugu District}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, to the southern limit represented by the Nakao Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. They are mainly distributed throughout the Miyazaki Plain, extending into basins in areas such as {{ill|Miyakonojō|en|Miyakonojō|WD=Q638301|lt=Tosu City}}, {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, and {{ill|Ebino, Miyazaki|en|Ebino, Miyazaki|WD=Q374701|lt=Ebino City}} at the northern foothills of the {{ill|Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja|霧島火山群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 霧島山|1=Mount Kirishima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1319361}}, with the western boundary defined by the Harumura Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in {{ill|Isa, Kagoshima|en|Isa, Kagoshima|WD=Q15736|lt=Isa City}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. Additionally, two tombs have been identified at the Tendōgao site in {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|WD=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, indicating that the northwestern extent of this tomb style reaches into the basin of the {{ill|Kuma River (Japan)|en|Kuma River (Japan)|WD=Q1358183|lt=Kumagawa River}}.
In total, more than 1,000 Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs have been discovered in Miyazaki and Kagoshima Prefectures,<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012"/> with over 300 confirmed in the Ebino City region of western Miyazaki Prefecture.
==Origins and Spread== In the latter half of the early Kofun period to the early mid-Kofun period, the “Yokuguchi-style earthen tomb” discovered within a subgroup of the {{ill|Kogihara Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja|小木原地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogihara Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}} is regarded as the initial form. Subsequently, the tombs became broadly classified into two types based on the shape of the burial chamber – the “houseform type” and the “earthen mound type” – which spread across various regions via regional transmission from the 5th through the 6th centuries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=143"/>
In the Miyazaki Plain and along the coast of the Ōsumi Peninsula at Shibushi Bay, the distribution area of keyhole-shaped tumuli overlaps with that of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs; similarly, in the inland areas near the Okuchi Basin, the distribution overlaps with that of another southern Kyushu burial system, the {{ill|stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓|1=stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|qq=}} (Underground stone slab tomb).
==Research History== Records of the discovery of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs date back to the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} and even earlier to the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治期|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}}. In the work ''{{ill|Keirin Manroku|ja|桂林漫録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keirin Manroku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'' by {{ill|Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja|森島（桂川）中良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the younger brother of {{ill|Katsuragawa Hoshū|en|Katsuragawa Hoshū|WD=Q946932|lt=Katsuragawa Hoshu}}, an account from 1789 (the 1st year of {{ill|Kansei|en|Kansei|WD=Q1195131|lt=Kansei}}) describes a farmer in {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}} near the pig mound at {{ill|Inoh-tsuka|ja|猪の塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inoh-tsuka|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|en|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132180|lt=Higashimorokata District}}, {{ill|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|en|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350786|lt=Kunimoto Town}}, Honjō) who, while digging a trench, encountered a horizontal cave whose walls were painted vermilion, from which numerous relics were unearthed. Local historian {{ill|Senokuchi Denkurō|ja|瀬之口伝九郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senokuchi Denkurō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} regarded this as the earliest literary reference to an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/> In modern times, archaeological research began to focus on these tombs; Senokuchi Denkurō coined the term “Underground-type Tomb” and classified it as one form of Kofun period burial system.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/>
Later, studies employing archaeological methods—such as the classification of plan and cross-sectional morphologies, chronological analyses based on grave good assemblages, and examinations of the relationship between these tombs and keyhole-shaped tumuli—progressed gradually.<ref name="Sfn|日高|1958"/><ref name="Sfn|石川|1973"/>
===The “Hayato Burial System” Theory=== In parallel, due to its unique structure, concentrated distribution in southern Kyushu, and the fact that southern Kyushu lay on the periphery of the keyhole-shaped tumuli (Kofun culture zone), some scholars proposed in literary sources that Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs were the tombs of the “Hayato,” a group considered peripheral or “other” by the ancient {{ill|Ritsuryō state|ja|律令国家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō state|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 律令制|1=ritsuryō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q742460}}. <ref name="Sfn|高橋|1924"/> In the 1960s–80s, as overall views of the Kofun period were synthesized, this theory accelerated, with various opinions emerging that identified Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs as the burial system of the “Hyūga–Ōsumi Hayato,” the Underground stone slab tomb as the burial system of the “Satsuma Hayato,” and the “Tateishi Doikombō” found in the southern Satsuma Peninsula as the burial system of the “Ata Hayato.”<ref name="Sfn|小田|1966|p=163"/><ref name="Sfn|乙益|1970"/><ref name="Sfn|上村|1984"/> Their formation was attributed to the fact that the area featured volcanic soils, limited flatlands unsuitable for rice cultivation, and an environment isolated from external influences, leading to a stagnation in cultural change since the Yayoi period and the establishment of an independent local sphere. This conceptualization of a “specialized underground tomb system in southern Kyushu” as representing the “Hayato tombs” – contrasting the expanding dominion of the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato court|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kinship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}} over the archipelago with the indigenous “non-Hayato” local forces – gained widespread acceptance.
However, by the 1990s, many researchers, particularly those from local Kyushu academic circles, began to question whether linking Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs with the “Hayato” was appropriate.
Literary sources first mention “Hayato” in the mythological sections of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}}, and the term appears from the time of Emperor Nintoku onward; however, it is generally accepted that the term “Hayato” began to be used as a confirmed historical designation only from the 11th month of the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmu period|ja|天武朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu period|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (682 AD, in records of Hayato tributary missions).<ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/> In contrast, the flourishing of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs is centered on the 5th to 6th centuries and appears to have persisted only until roughly the mid-7th century. Moreover, the territories inhabited by groups referred to as “Hayato” during the Ritsuryō period were confined to {{ill|Ōsumi Province|en|Ōsumi Province|WD=Q981002|lt=Ōsumi Province}} and {{ill|Satsuma Province|ja|Satsuma Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satsuma Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, excluding {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}}. Therefore, if the distribution of a common tomb style reflects the habitation area of a culturally unified group, then while the local inhabitants of Osumi may be considered “Hayato,” those of Hyūga would not. It is argued that the very concept of “Hayato” was a pseudo-ethnic construct, politically and arbitrarily created by the Ritsuryō government based on Sinocentric ideology, rather than a notion arising from indigenous differences.<ref name="Sfn|永山|2009|pp=40"/><ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/><ref name="Sfn|東|2001|p=498"/>
Archaeologically, numerous instances have been documented in which keyhole-shaped tumuli and Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs coexist, or where Underground Tombs constitute the primary burial facility within keyhole-shaped tumuli, evidencing a relationship that cannot be explained solely by a dichotomy of “Yamato” versus “local forces.” Consequently, the simplistic equation of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs with “Hayato tombs” has gradually fallen out of favor in both archaeological and literary studies.<ref name="Sfn|下山|1995"/><ref name="Sfn|永山|1998|pp=10–11"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2008"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2011"/>
===Research After the “Hayato Burial System” Theory=== From the 2000s onward, research on Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs has increasingly utilized the vast array of excavation data and artifacts to examine these tombs through rigorous archaeological methodologies—as a regional burial system of the Kofun period. Detailed discussions now focus on classifications based on structural morphology, chronological models derived from grave good assemblages and distribution patterns, and analyses of the social structures within regions where these tombs were constructed in relation to keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|第4回九州前方後円墳研究会|2001"/><ref name="Sfn|第6回九州前方後円墳研究会|2003"/>
Current understanding increasingly supports the view that the emergence, development, and spread of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs resulted from the adoption of “horizontal cave–type” burial technology (in both funerary concept and technique) brought from the continent, implemented in an underground structure. This indicates that rather than arising in isolation in a secluded environment, this tomb style was established through active regional exchange with the {{ill|Korean Peninsula|ja|朝鮮半島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Korean Peninsula|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Korean Peninsula|WD=Q483134}} and the {{ill|Yamato government|ja|ヤマト政権|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato government|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kinship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}}, and thus should not be seen as a product of isolation.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012"/>

===Kagoshima Prefecture=== * {{ill|Shinryō Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja|神領地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shinryō Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in Shinryō and Yokose, {{ill|Ōsaki, Kagoshima|en|Ōsaki, Kagoshima|WD=Q931439|lt=Osaki Town}}, {{ill|Soo District, Kagoshima|en|Soo District, Kagoshima|WD=Q1043870|lt=So District}}) – situated within the Shinryō Kofun Group and coexisting with it. * {{ill|Okazaki Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja|岡崎地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okazaki Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in Okazaki, {{ill|Kushira, Kagoshima|en|Kushira, Kagoshima|WD=Q6447960|lt=Kushira Town}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City}}) – situated within the Okazaki Kofun Group and coexisting with it. * {{ill|Nakao Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja|中尾地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nakao Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in Kamina Nakao, {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City}}) – a tomb group located at the southern limit of the main distribution area.
===Kumamoto Prefecture=== * {{ill|Tendōgao Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja|天道ヶ尾地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tendōgao Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in Tendōgao, {{ill|Nanase Town|ja|七地町|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Nanase Town|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City}}) – two Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs discovered at the Tendōgao site; although somewhat removed from the main distribution area, they mark the northwestern limit of this tomb style.
==Funerary Goods== The most commonly recovered grave goods include iron weapons such as swords, bows, and arrows, and earthenware items such as {{ill|Haji pottery|en|Haji pottery|WD=Q5639938|lt=Haji pottery}} and {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}, with iron arrowheads—particularly those of the {{ill|Keitō type|ja|圭頭鏃|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keitō type|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}—appearing very frequently. Additionally, items such as {{ill|snake-like swords|ja|蛇行剣|1=Dakōken|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/snake-like swords|13=User:Immanuelle/Dakōken|qq=}} and various irregularly shaped iron implements are characteristic. There are also cases where especially luxurious grave goods, including jade objects, armor ({{ill|Japanese armour|en|Japanese armour|WD=Q3671179|lt=kacchū}}), equestrian gear ({{ill|Horse tack|en|Horse tack|WD=Q950799|lt=horse gear}}), and mirrors, are interred; tombs containing such goods are considered comparable to elite head tombs found in keyhole-shaped Kofuns.
==Distribution== The distribution of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs extends from the northern limit at the Ushimoku Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in Ōaza Kamie, {{ill|Takanabe, Miyazaki|en|Takanabe, Miyazaki|WD=Q1206737|lt=Takanabe Town}}, {{ill|Koyu District, Miyazaki|en|Koyu District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132169|lt=Koyugu District}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, to the southern limit at the Nakao Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. They are mainly distributed in the Miyazaki Plain, extending into the basins of areas such as {{ill|Miyakonojō|en|Miyakonojō|WD=Q638301|lt=Tosu City}}, {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, and {{ill|Ebino, Miyazaki|en|Ebino, Miyazaki|WD=Q374701|lt=Ebino City}} at the northern foothills of the {{ill|Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja|霧島火山群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 霧島山|1=Mount Kirishima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1319361}}, with the western boundary marked by the Harumura Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in {{ill|Isa, Kagoshima|en|Isa, Kagoshima|WD=Q15736|lt=Isa City}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. Additionally, two tombs have been detected at the Tendōgao site in {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|WD=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, indicating that the northwestern extent of this tomb style reaches into the basin of the {{ill|Kuma River (Japan)|en|Kuma River (Japan)|WD=Q1358183|lt=Kumagawa River}}.
In total, more than 1,000 Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs have been discovered in Miyazaki and Kagoshima Prefectures,<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012"/> with over 300 confirmed in the Ebino City region of western Miyazaki Prefecture.
==Origins and Spread== The initial form of the tomb is thought to be the “Yokuguchi-style Earthen Tomb” that appeared in the latter half of the early Kofun period to the early mid-Kofun period, discovered within a subgroup of the {{ill|Kogihara Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja|小木原地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogihara Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}. Thereafter, based on the shape of the burial chamber, these tombs were broadly classified into two categories – the “houseform type” and the “earthen mound type” – which spread across various regions via transmission from the 5th to the 6th centuries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=143"/>
In the Miyazaki Plain and along the coast of the Ōsumi Peninsula at Shibushi Bay, the distribution of keyhole-shaped tumuli overlaps with that of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs; in the inland areas near the Okuchi Basin, their distribution overlaps with that of another southern Kyushu burial style, the {{ill|stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓|1=stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|qq=}} (Underground stone slab tomb).
==Research History== Records of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs date back to the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} and even earlier to the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治期|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}}. In the work ''{{ill|Keirin Manroku|ja|桂林漫録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keirin Manroku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'' by {{ill|Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja|森島（桂川）中良|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the younger brother of {{ill|Katsuragawa Hoshū|en|Katsuragawa Hoshū|WD=Q946932|lt=Katsuragawa Hoshu}}, an account from 1789 (the 1st year of {{ill|Kansei|en|Kansei|WD=Q1195131|lt=Kansei}}) describes a farmer in {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}} near the pig mound at {{ill|Inoh-tsuka|ja|猪の塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Inoh-tsuka|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (located in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|en|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132180|lt=Higashimorokata District}}, {{ill|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|en|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350786|lt=Kunimoto Town}}, Honjō) who, while digging a trench, encountered a horizontal cave with its walls painted vermilion, from which numerous relics were unearthed. Local historian {{ill|Senokuchi Denkurō|ja|瀬之口伝九郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senokuchi Denkurō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} regarded this as the earliest literary reference to an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/> In modern times, research in the field of {{ill|Archaeology|en|Archaeology|WD=Q23498|lt=archaeology}} began, and Senokuchi Denkurō coined the term “Underground-type Tomb” to classify it as one form of Kofun period burial system.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/>
Subsequently, studies have gradually advanced using archaeological methods such as the classification of plan and cross-sectional morphologies, chronological analyses based on grave goods, and examinations of the relationship between these tombs and keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|日高|1958"/><ref name="Sfn|石川|1973"/>
===The “Hayato Burial System” Theory=== Alongside these developments, a theory emerged proposing that Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs, due to their unique structure, concentrated distribution in southern Kyushu, and the fact that southern Kyushu lay on the periphery of the keyhole-shaped tumuli (Kofun culture zone), were the tombs of the “Hayato,” a group historically considered peripheral by the ancient {{ill|Ritsuryō state|ja|律令国家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō state|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 律令制|1=ritsuryō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q742460}}. <ref name="Sfn|高橋|1924"/> In the 1960s–80s, as comprehensive views of the Kofun period emerged, this theory accelerated, with several scholars identifying Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs as representing the burial system of the “Hyūga–Ōsumi Hayato,” the Underground stone slab tomb as that of the “Satsuma Hayato,” and certain tumuli-associated tombs in the southern Satsuma Peninsula as that of the “Ata Hayato.”<ref name="Sfn|小田|1966|p=163"/><ref name="Sfn|乙益|1970"/><ref name="Sfn|上村|1984"/> Their formation was attributed to the region’s volcanic soils, limited flatlands unsuitable for rice cultivation, and its isolation from external influences, leading to cultural stagnation from the Yayoi period onward and the establishment of an independent local sphere. This framework, which depicted the “specialized underground tomb system in southern Kyushu” as “Hayato tombs” in contrast to the expanding dominion of the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato court|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kinship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}}, gradually gained widespread acceptance.
However, by the 1990s, increasing criticism emerged—especially from scholars in Kyushu—questioning the appropriateness of linking Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs with the “Hayato.”
The term “Hayato” first appears in the mythological portions of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}}, and while it is mentioned from the time of Emperor Nintoku, its use as a confirmed historical term is generally recognized only from the 11th month of the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmu period|ja|天武朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu period|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (682 AD, in records of Hayato tributary missions).<ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/> In contrast, the peak of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs was in the 5th to 6th centuries, and they appear to have largely ceased by the mid-7th century. Furthermore, the areas inhabited by groups identified as “Hayato” during the Ritsuryō period were confined to {{ill|Ōsumi Province|en|Ōsumi Province|WD=Q981002|lt=Ōsumi Province}} and {{ill|Satsuma Province|ja|Satsuma Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satsuma Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, excluding {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}}. Thus, if the common burial system reflects a unified cultural group, the inhabitants of Osumi might be considered “Hayato,” whereas those of Hyūga would not. It is argued that the very notion of “Hayato” was a pseudo-ethnic construct, politically created by the Ritsuryō government based on Sinocentric ideology rather than arising from indigenous ethnic differences.<ref name="Sfn|永山|2009|pp=40"/><ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/><ref name="Sfn|東|2001|p=498"/>
Archaeologically, numerous instances have been documented where keyhole-shaped tumuli and Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs coexist, or where Underground Tombs serve as the main burial facility within tumuli, indicating that their relationship cannot be simply explained as a dichotomy between “Yamato” and local forces. Consequently, the equation of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs with “Hayato tombs” has gradually lost support in both archaeological and literary studies.<ref name="Sfn|下山|1995"/><ref name="Sfn|永山|1998|pp=10–11"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2008"/><ref name="Sfn|原口|2011"/>
===Research After the “Hayato Burial System” Theory=== From the 2000s onward, research on Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs has increasingly employed extensive excavation data and artifacts to examine these tombs using rigorous archaeological methods, viewing them as a regional burial system of the Kofun period. Detailed discussions now focus on classifications based on structural morphology, chronological models derived from grave goods and distribution patterns, and analyses of the social structure of the regions where these tombs were constructed in relation to keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|第4回九州前方後円墳研究会|2001"/><ref name="Sfn|第6回九州前方後円墳研究会|2003"/>

<!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:地下式横穴墓]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:地下式横穴墓]] <!--interwikis from wikidata-->[[ja:地下式横穴墓]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q11424056]] Wikidata name: underground tunnel tomb [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:16, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} [[File:地下式横穴墓の模式図.png|350px|thumb|{{ill|Schematic diagram of an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb|ja|地下式横穴墓の模式図|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Schematic diagram of an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}]] '''Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb''' (地下式横穴墓) is a tomb in which a vertical pit is excavated into the ground, and from that pit a horizontal chamber is dug to construct a burial facility in which the deceased are interred. It is known as a regionally distinctive burial style that appeared during the 5th to 6th centuries of the {{ill|Kofun period|en|Kofun period|WD=Q459939|lt=Kofun period}} in southern parts of the {{ill|Kyushu region|ja|九州地方|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kyushu region|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 九州|1=Kyushu|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q13987}}, particularly from the southern part of {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}} to the eastern part of {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}.
==Overview== The Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb is situated in the flatlands of the upper portion of a plateau, in contrast to the more widespread {{ill|cave tomb|lt=horizontal cave tombs|ja|横穴墓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/cave tomb|qq=}} of the mid to late Kofun period, which were built by excavating into hillsides or cliff faces. In the Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb, a vertical pit is dug to a depth of approximately 2–3 meters, and then excavation proceeds horizontally from the bottom of the pit, ensuring that the burial chamber is constructed at a level below the surface. Thus, by contrast with standard horizontal cave tombs, the term “underground type” is applied.
===Structure=== ; Vertical Pit : The vertical pit (also written as “竪穴”) generally has a plan form that is roughly elliptical or quadrangular with rounded corners and serves as the entrance descending underground. It is speculated that a ladder or similar apparatus was used for ascent and descent; for example, in one Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb at Tomb No. 18 of the {{ill|Okazaki Kofun Group|ja|岡崎古墳群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Okazaki Kofun Group|1=Okazaki Kofun Group|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q42581362}} in {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City}}, {{ill|foot-holds|ja|足掛け|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/foot-holds|1=foot-holds|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11636886}} were detected on the wall of the pit. Since burial rites in these tombs often involved secondary interments, the vertical pit was typically not refilled, remaining open or sealed at its top with flagstones or wooden boards. ; Access Passage : The portion leading from the bottom of the vertical pit to the burial chamber is called the “access passage” (羨道); however, when its length is too short to be considered a “passage,” it is sometimes referred to as the “access gate” (羨門). The entrance to the access passage was sealed by stacking flagstones, river stones, or lumps of clay. ; Burial Chamber : The burial chamber (玄室) is excavated as a broad horizontal space deeper within the access passage. Its plan may vary – it can be a long rectangular chamber (wife-entry type), a nearly square chamber, a chamber with a width disproportionately greater than its depth (plain-entry type), or even an elliptical chamber. Some chambers have a domed ceiling, while others feature a triangular ceiling that clearly mimics the roof of a house, decorated with motifs resembling pillars, beams, or horizontal lintels. The remains were interred in an extended posture from the rear of the chamber, and with each subsequent secondary burial the newly interred were placed nearer the entrance. In some cases, during secondary burial, previously interred remains that had become ossified were relocated to the rear wall corner to make room. In certain tombs, the remains were placed directly on the floor; in others, a mortuary platform of rounded stones or a Sarcophagus constructed with flagstones was provided. Alongside the remains, grave goods such as iron weapons, {{ill|Haji pottery|en|Haji pottery|WD=Q5639938|lt=Haji pottery}} and {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}, as well as ornaments, were deposited. Owing to the sealed nature of the underground chamber, these grave goods have generally been preserved in relatively good condition at the time of excavation, largely free from soil degradation and later looting. ; Surface Structures : Generally, there are no surface structures or markers resembling the tumuli of keyhole-shaped Kofuns present on the ground surface. Consequently, the locations of these tombs often went unrecognized by later generations; there are instances where collapse of the burial chamber ceiling led to sudden ground subsidence and subsequent discovery, or where plowing or agricultural improvements caused farm animals or tractors to become caught in a collapsed chamber, leading to accidental discoveries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=139"/> In recent times, surveys of buried cultural assets have sometimes employed ground-penetrating radar to determine the location. Additionally, the {{ill|Board of Education of Miyazaki City|ja|宮崎県都城市|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Board of Education of Miyazaki City|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} has issued warnings on its website regarding sudden ground subsidence in agricultural areas, noting that such events may indicate the presence of an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb.
===Group Structure=== An individual Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb is rarely constructed alone; they are usually found in clusters of 2–3 or even in groups of over 100. Consequently, the archaeological site is typically designated as “[Place Name] + Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group.” Moreover, as mentioned above, there are examples where several Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs form a circular group, or where vertical pits are excavated at the base of tumuli such as keyhole-shaped mounds (【前方後円墳】), with the burial chamber oriented toward the summit of the mound, appearing as if subordinate to or sharing the mound.
==Funerary Goods== The most commonly recovered funerary goods include iron weapons such as swords and bows and arrows, as well as earthenware items such as {{ill|Haji pottery|en|Haji pottery|WD=Q5639938|lt=Haji pottery}} and {{ill|Sue pottery|en|Sue pottery|WD=Q7634351|lt=Sue pottery}}; notably, iron arrowheads are frequently found, with the majority being of the {{ill|Keitō arrowhead|ja|圭頭鏃|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keitō arrowhead|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} type. Additionally, there are cases where exceptionally luxurious grave goods – including jewelry, armor ({{ill|Japanese armour|en|Japanese armour|WD=Q3671179|lt=kacchū}}), equestrian gear ({{ill|Horse tack|en|Horse tack|WD=Q950799|lt=magugu}}), and mirrors – have been interred. Tombs containing such lavish goods are considered comparable to elite head tombs found in keyhole-shaped Kofuns.
==Distribution== The distribution of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs extends from the northern limit at the Ushimoku Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in the Ōaza Kamie of {{ill|Takanabe, Miyazaki|en|Takanabe, Miyazaki|WD=Q1206737|lt=Takanabe Town}}, {{ill|Koyu District, Miyazaki|en|Koyu District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132169|lt=Koyugu District}} in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, to the southern limit at the Nakao Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in {{ill|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|en|Aira, Kagoshima (Kimotsuki District)|WD=Q4698402|lt=Awa-cho, Agata}}, {{ill|Kanoya, Kagoshima|en|Kanoya, Kagoshima|WD=Q819578|lt=Kanoya City}} in {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}}. They are distributed in the basins of the Miyazaki Plain and extend into areas such as {{ill|Miyakonojō|en|Miyakonojō|WD=Q638301|lt=Tosu City}}, {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, and {{ill|Ebino, Miyazaki|en|Ebino, Miyazaki|WD=Q374701|lt=Ebino City}}, at the northern foothills of the {{ill|Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja|霧島火山群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kirishima Volcanic Group|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 霧島山|1=Mount Kirishima|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1319361}}, with the western limit marked by the Harumura Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group in {{ill|Isa, Kagoshima|en|Isa, Kagoshima|WD=Q15736|lt=Isa City}}, {{ill|Kagoshima Prefecture|en|Kagoshima Prefecture|WD=Q15701|lt=Kagoshima Prefecture}} on the western slope of Kirishima. On the Ōsumi Peninsula, they are found along the coast of {{ill|Shibushi Bay|ja|志布志湾|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Shibushi Bay|1=Shibushi Bay|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q11490886}} from {{ill|Kushima, Miyazaki|en|Kushima, Miyazaki|WD=Q845800|lt=Kushima City}} in {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}} to {{ill|Ōsaki, Kagoshima|en|Ōsaki, Kagoshima|WD=Q931439|lt=Osaki Town}} in {{ill|Soo District, Kagoshima|en|Soo District, Kagoshima|WD=Q1043870|lt=Soo District}}, as well as within the inland area of Kanoya City. Slightly removed from the main distribution areas, two tombs have been detected at the Tendōgao site in {{ill|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|en|Hitoyoshi, Kumamoto|WD=Q861292|lt=Hitoyoshi City}}, {{ill|Kumamoto Prefecture|en|Kumamoto Prefecture|WD=Q130308|lt=Kumamoto Prefecture}}, indicating that the northwestern limit of this tomb style extends into the basin of the {{ill|Kuma River (Japan)|en|Kuma River (Japan)|WD=Q1358183|lt=Kumagawa River}}.
The total number of tombs discovered in both Miyazaki and Kagoshima Prefectures exceeds 1,000,<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012"/> with over 300 confirmed in the Ebino City region of western Miyazaki Prefecture.
==Origins and Spread== In the early form of the tomb, the “Yokuguchi-style earthen tomb” that emerged in the latter half of the early Kofun period in a subgroup within the {{ill|Kogihara Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja|小木原地下式横穴墓群|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kogihara Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb Group|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} in {{ill|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|en|Kobayashi, Miyazaki|WD=Q861283|lt=Kobayashi City}}, {{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, is considered to be the precursor. Subsequently, based on the shape of the burial chamber, these tombs became broadly categorized into two types – the “houseform type” and the “earthen mound type” – which were transmitted across various prefectures from the 5th to the 6th centuries.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012|p=143"/>
In the Miyazaki Plain and along the coast of Shibushi Bay on the Ōsumi Peninsula, the distribution area of keyhole-shaped tumuli overlaps with that of the Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs, and in the inland areas near the Okuchi Basin, the distribution of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs overlaps with that of another southern Kyushu burial style, the {{ill|stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓|1=stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|qq=}} (Underground stone slab tomb).
==Research History== The discovery records of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs date back from the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} to the {{ill|Meiji period|ja|明治期|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Meiji period|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 明治|1=Meiji period|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q3125096}}, with an account in the work ''{{ill|Keirin Manroku|ja|桂林漫録|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Keirin Manroku|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}'' by {{ill|Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja|森島（桂川）中良|lt=Mori Island Nakayoshi|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Mori Island Nakayoshi|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, the younger brother of {{ill|Katsuragawa Hoshū|en|Katsuragawa Hoshū|WD=Q946932|lt=Katsuragawa Hoshu}}, noting that in 1789 (the 1st year of {{ill|Kansei|en|Kansei|WD=Q1195131|lt=Kansei}}) a farmer in {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}} near {{ill|Ino-tsuka|ja|猪の塚|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ino-tsuka|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} ({{ill|Miyazaki Prefecture|en|Miyazaki Prefecture|WD=Q130300|lt=Miyazaki Prefecture}}, {{ill|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|en|Higashimorokata District, Miyazaki|WD=Q1132180|lt=Higashimorokata District}}, {{ill|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|en|Kunitomi, Miyazaki|WD=Q1350786|lt=Kunimoto Town}}, Honjō) discovered a horizontal cave with its walls painted vermilion, from which numerous relics were unearthed. Local historian {{ill|Senokuchi Denkurō|ja|瀬之口伝九郎|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Senokuchi Denkurō|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} regarded this as the first literary reference to an Underground Horizontal Cave Tomb.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/> In modern times, research in the field of {{ill|Archaeology|en|Archaeology|WD=Q23498|lt=archaeology}} began, and it was Senokuchi Denkurō who coined the term “Underground-type Tomb” and framed it as one form of Kofun period burial style.<ref name="Sfn|瀬之口|1919"/>
Subsequently, archaeological studies employing methods such as plan and cross-sectional classification of the remains, chronological investigations based on grave goods, and analyses of the relationship between these tombs and keyhole-shaped tumuli have gradually advanced.<ref name="Sfn|日高|1958"/><ref name="Sfn|石川|1973"/>
===The “Hayato Burial System” Theory=== Parallel to these developments, a theory emerged suggesting that Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs, owing to their peculiar structure, their concentrated distribution in southern Kyushu, and the fact that southern Kyushu lay on the periphery of the keyhole-shaped tumuli distribution (the Kofun cultural sphere), were the tombs of the “Hayato” – a group regarded in ancient literature as peripheral or “other” tribes by the centralized {{ill|Ritsuryō state|ja|律令国家|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Ritsuryō state|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 律令制|1=ritsuryō|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q742460}}. <ref name="Sfn|高橋|1924"/> In the 1960s–80s, as comprehensive studies of Kofun period society emerged, this theory accelerated, and several researchers posited that Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs represented the burial system of the “Hyūga–Ōsumi Hayato”, that the {{ill|stone slab tomb|ja|板石積石棺墓|1=stone slab tomb|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|13=User:Immanuelle/stone slab tomb|qq=}} (Underground stone slab tomb) represented the burial system of the “Satsuma Hayato”, and that the “Tateishi Doikombō” found in the southern part of the Satsuma Peninsula represented the burial system of the “Ata Hayato”.<ref name="Sfn|小田|1966|p=163"/><ref name="Sfn|乙益|1970"/><ref name="Sfn|上村|1984"/> Their formation was explained by the fact that the area was characterized by volcanic soils, limited plains unsuitable for rice cultivation, and an environment isolated from the outside world, which resulted in the stagnation of cultural change from the Yayoi period onward and the emergence of an independent local power sphere. This view, portraying a dichotomy between the expanding dominion of the {{ill|Yamato court|ja|大和朝廷|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato court|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kinship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}} (centered in the Kofun cultural sphere) and the “Hayato” – a group created politically and arbitrarily by the Ritsuryō government based on {{ill|Sinocentric ideology|ja|華夷思想|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Sinocentric ideology|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 中華思想|1=sinocentrism|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q1370788}} – became widely accepted among the general public.
However, from the 1990s onward, many researchers – especially local scholars and academic circles in Kyushu – began to question whether linking Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs with the “Hayato” was appropriate.
In literary sources, the first appearance of the term “Hayato” is found in the mythological sections of the {{ill|Kojiki|en|Kojiki|WD=Q813031|lt=Kojiki}}, and it appears from the reign of Emperor Nintoku onward; yet as a confirmed historical fact, the use of the term “Hayato” is generally accepted only from the 11th month of the 11th year of the {{ill|Tenmu period|ja|天武朝|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tenmu period|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (682 AD, in records of Hayato tributes) onward.<ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/> In contrast, the heyday of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs was centered on the 5th to 6th centuries, and they persisted only until roughly the mid-7th century. Moreover, the territories inhabited by the groups referred to as “Hayato” during the Ritsuryō period were limited to {{ill|Ōsumi Province|en|Ōsumi Province|WD=Q981002|lt=Ōsumi Province}} and {{ill|Satsuma Province|ja|Satsuma Province|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Satsuma Province|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}, excluding {{ill|Hyūga Province|en|Hyūga Province|WD=Q513737|lt=Hyūga Province}}; if the distribution of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs indeed indicates the habitation of a culturally unified group, then while the inhabitants of Osumi may be considered “Hayato,” those of Hyūga would not. It is argued that the very notion of “Hayato” was a pseudo-ethnic construct created by the Ritsuryō government based on Sinocentric ideology, rather than a concept arising from indigenous power or ethnic differences.<ref name="Sfn|永山|2009|pp=40"/><ref name="Sfn|中村|1993"/><ref name="Sfn|東|2001|p=498"/>
From an archaeological standpoint, numerous examples have emerged in which keyhole-shaped tumuli and Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs coexisted, or where Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs served as the primary burial facility within keyhole-shaped tumuli, indicating that the relationship between these two burial styles cannot be adequately explained by a simple dichotomy of “Yamato” versus “local forces.” In this context, the simplistic equation of Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs with “Hayato tombs” has increasingly come under criticism.
===Research After the “Hayato Burial System” Theory=== From the 2000s onward, research on Underground Horizontal Cave Tombs has increasingly employed the vast amount of data and artifacts recovered from excavations to examine these tombs in a more archaeological manner as a regional burial system of the Kofun period. Detailed discussions have emerged regarding classification based on structural typology, chronological models derived from grave good assemblages and distribution patterns, and analyses of the social structure of regions where Underground Tombs were constructed in relation to keyhole-shaped tumuli.<ref name="Sfn|第4回九州前方後円墳研究会|2001"/><ref name="Sfn|第6回九州前方後円墳研究会|2003"/>
Currently, it is becoming increasingly clear that the emergence, development, and spread of this tomb style resulted from the adoption of “horizontal cave–type” burial techniques (both in funerary ideology and technology) brought from the continent. In this region, these techniques were implemented in an underground structure, indicating that this tomb style was not born in isolation in an inhospitable environment but was established through active regional exchange with the {{ill|Korean Peninsula|ja|朝鮮半島|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Korean Peninsula|comment=changed title based on wikidata|1=Korean Peninsula|WD=Q483134}} and the {{ill|Yamato government|ja|ヤマト政権|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yamato government|ja_comment=|2=ja|3=ヤマト王権|1=Yamato Kinship|comment=changed title based on wikidata|WD=Q2658252}}.<ref name="Sfn|橋本|2012"/>
